conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___ from Orthopedics. You were brought in after a fall from your wheelchair four days ago. We’ve reviewed your X-rays and found fractures in your right hip and leg. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m in a lot of pain, especially in my right leg. I didn’t think it was this bad when it happened, but the swelling got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve started you on pain medication to help. The X-rays show a fracture near your hip — that’s called an intertrochanteric femur fracture — and another in your tibia and fibula, the bones in your lower leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery? I’m worried about complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that with the team. Because you’re already non-weight-bearing due to your paraplegia, and because of your other health conditions, the risks of surgery outweigh the benefits. We’re treating this non-operatively with bracing and careful monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But will the bones heal properly without surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may take longer, but with proper immobilization and care, they can heal. We’ve already done a closed reduction in the ER to realign the bones, and the follow-up X-ray shows improved alignment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my UTI? My primary doctor just started me on Augmentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing that. You have a history of recurrent UTIs, so we want to make sure this one clears up. We’ll keep you on the amoxicillin-clavulanate, which is similar to Augmentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had bad reactions to some antibiotics before. I’m allergic to Bactrim and Cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ve reviewed your allergies — you’re allergic to Bactrim, Levaquin, Vancomycin, and several others. We’ll avoid those completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my seizures — I take levetiracetam regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your levetiracetam. No seizure activity noted since admission. We’ll keep that up to prevent any episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been anxious lately. Is it okay if I keep taking my anxiety meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added alprazolam to your discharge plan for anxiety, as needed. We’ll monitor how you’re doing, but it’s safe to use with your other medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. What about blood clots? I’ve heard that’s a risk when you can’t move much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent point. We did an ultrasound to check for deep vein thrombosis. The results were negative — no clots found in your legs. But to prevent any from forming, we’re starting enoxaparin, a blood thinner, for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to give that to myself? I can’t feel my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a daily injection under the skin. A home health nurse will come to help you with it, and train your caregiver if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about my kidney? I have CKD, and some meds can hurt it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. Your baseline creatinine is known, and we’ve adjusted your sevelamer dose accordingly. We’re avoiding any nephrotoxic drugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain meds — I was on oxycodone before. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting your pain regimen. You’ll be on a lower-dose extended-release oxycodone, plus a smaller dose as needed. We’re being cautious due to your history and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I wanted to update you — we repeated the X-rays after casting, and the alignment of your tibia and fibula is stable. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the brace supposed to stay on all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it must stay locked in extension at all times. You should not remove it. Also, check the skin under the brace daily — we don’t want pressure sores, especially with your history of MRSA ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ll have my mom help with that. She’s been managing my care for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll also have a home health nurse visit to assist with wound checks and injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been feeling a bit anxious about going home. Will I be able to manage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with home health services, physical therapy, and nursing support. You’ll have help with meds, injections, and mobility. And you’re going home with a new wheelchair with elevating leg rests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Can I sit up in the wheelchair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can be out of bed in the wheelchair with assistance. But you must remain non-weight-bearing on the right leg. Keep it elevated to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No walking on it — not that I could anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is better controlled now, and your swelling is improving. We’re planning for discharge in the next couple of days if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds will I be going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue docusate and senna for bowel management, levetiracetam for seizures, pantoprazole for stomach protection, and amlodipine for blood pressure. Plus the enoxaparin, antibiotics, and pain meds we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sleep? I’ve been using Ambien.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to zolpidem, which is similar, and also allowing trazodone or clonazepam as needed. We want to minimize sedatives but help you rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw the X-ray report mentioned a joint effusion. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s some fluid in the knee joint, likely from the injury. It’s not unusual and should resolve as the fracture heals. We’re watching it, but no intervention is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the osteopenia mentioned — is that related to my paraplegia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, prolonged immobility can lead to bone thinning. That’s why healing may take longer. We’ll discuss long-term bone health with your primary doctor later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today. You’re in stable condition, pain is controlled, and your fractures are stable without surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the brace on, elevate your leg, don’t bear weight, and check your skin daily. Continue all meds, especially the enoxaparin for four weeks. Avoid alcohol and driving while on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see orthopedics in two weeks. Physical therapy will start at home. Call us if you develop fever, redness, increased pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, follow the instructions, and you’ll do well. The home health team will be there this afternoon.
